we-the-people-1787-1791.works: The population pies are big and their colours match the Spanish sheet (blue for free people, orange-red for enslaved people), and every pop-up title gives the state name, so I can find each state without place names. Short lines like 'plus 2 senators, like every state' and '194 for, 77 against' are easy for me to read.

findings.where: q4-ratify and q4-nc pictures; layer Ratifying the Constitution, 1787–1791; Q4 (¿Qué tan reñida fue la ratificación?) steps 3–4, and the 'Cómo leer el mapa' note that the labels give the order
findings.what: I look for 'NC' to find Carolina del Norte. The label 'NC (1788)' is printed on a half-orange pie that is in Virginia, and 'NC 12' is next to a different pie that is mostly orange. 'SC 8' sits beside a pie in North Carolina. Every label is a little up and to the right of its own pie, so it touches the next pie up the coast. I click the pie under the label and the pop-up says a different state.
findings.why: There are no place names, so the labels are my only way to find a state without clicking every pie. When a label touches the wrong pie I have to click around and read each English title, and I can write down the wrong order or the wrong votes.
findings.suggestion: Centre each ratification label under its own pie, or add a short leader line from label to pie. If the offset has to stay, the sheet could add: 'La etiqueta está arriba a la derecha de su gráfico; confirma el estado en el título de la ventana emergente.'
findings.evidence: we-the-people-1787-1791--q4-ratify.png ('NC (1788)' on the pie at Richmond, 'NC 12' beside the Hillsborough pie, 'SC 8' beside the Fayetteville pie, 'GA 4' up and right of the small Augusta pie); we-the-people-1787-1791--q4-nc.png (the selected North Carolina pie has 'SC 8' printed just below and right of it)

findings.where: q2-seats picture; layer House seats in 1793, plus the Ratifying the Constitution pies and labels, which are drawn in this picture although the legend lists only House seats and Population; Q2 (Escaños en el Congreso) step 2, also Q3 step 2
findings.what: The sheet says each label gives the state and its seats. I see 'NY: 10' and also 'NY 11', 'PA: 13' and also 'PA 2', 'VA: 19' and 'VA 10', 'NC: 10' and 'NC 12', 'GA: 2' and 'GA 4', and then 'VT 14', 'RI 13', 'NH 9'. They look the same except for the colon. So did Rhode Island have 13 seats, and Pennsylvania 2?
findings.why: Numbers are easier for me than English sentences, so I trust the labels. Two sets of labels that look the same give me two answers for one state. The ones with no colon are the ratification order, not seats, so I could write that Vermont had 14 seats.
findings.suggestion: Check why the ratification pies and labels draw when House seats in 1793 is on; that layer should stay off until Q4. Make the two label styles clearly different: seats as 'NY: 10 seats', and ratification order as '11th' or '#11' in a different colour or style.
findings.evidence: we-the-people-1787-1791--q2-seats.png; the legend text for that view lists only House seats in 1793 and Population in 1790

findings.where: q2-seats picture; House seats in 1793 labels; Q2 step 2 and the question '¿cuál tenía menos?'
findings.what: I can read seat labels only for NY, PA, VA, KY, NC, GA and CT. Delaware, New Jersey, Maryland, Rhode Island, Vermont, New Hampshire and South Carolina have no seat label that I can see, and Massachusetts is under the pop-up. The lightest blue ('1 to 2 seats') covers several states.
findings.why: The state with the fewest seats is one of the tiny ones with no label. I have to find and click small states that have no names, and I don't know where Delaware is.
findings.suggestion: The map already has the bookmarks 'New England and New York' and 'The South'. Q2 on the sheet could add: 'Abre los marcadores New England and New York y The South para leer las etiquetas de los estados pequeños.' Or let the seat labels show at this scale with a smaller font or leader lines.
findings.evidence: we-the-people-1787-1791--q2-seats.png; bookmarks listed in the app: The states in 1790, New England and New York, The South

findings.where: q1-virginia pop-up (Population in 1790; the same text opens with House seats on); Q3 (La cláusula de los tres quintos) step 2
findings.what: The sheet tells me to read 'las dos últimas líneas' to find the seats if everyone or no one was counted. The last lines of the pop-up are about Kentucky and 'Seats: National Archives · Ratio: U.S. Census Bureau'. The numbers I need ('If enslaved people had been counted in full: 22 seats. If they had not been counted at all: 13 seats.') are in the middle, and the box is cut off, so I have to scroll.
findings.why: I follow the Spanish steps exactly, so I look at the bottom and find a note and the sources instead of numbers. 'Counted in full' and 'had not been counted at all' are hard grammar for me, so I'm not sure I've found the right sentence.
findings.suggestion: Change the sheet to 'luego el tercer párrafo, que empieza con If enslaved people…', or move that paragraph to the end of the pop-up. Simpler pop-up English would also help: 'All enslaved people counted: 22 seats. No enslaved people counted: 13 seats.'
findings.evidence: Pop-up text 'Virginia in 1790' (q1-virginia); we-the-people-1787-1791--q1-virginia.png shows the box cut off at 'West Virginia as part'

findings.where: q1-virginia pop-up; Population in 1790; Q1 (¿Quién vivía dónde en 1790?) step 3
findings.what: The first line says '(39.099998474121094%)'. Is that 39 percent? The number is very long.
findings.why: I have to stop and work out the number before I can say whether it is more than a quarter (una cuarta parte).
findings.suggestion: Round the percentage in the pop-up to a whole number or one decimal place (39.1%).
findings.evidence: Pop-up text: '1790 census: 747,610 people, 292,627 of them enslaved (39.099998474121094%).'

findings.where: All views; Q3 step 1 (Virginia y Carolina del Sur), Q4 step 4 (Carolina del Norte), and 'Cómo leer el mapa' (Virginia Occidental)
findings.what: My sheet says 'Carolina del Sur' and 'Carolina del Norte'. The map labels say 'SC' and 'NC', and the pop-ups say 'South Carolina' and 'North Carolina'. I have to guess that SC is Carolina del Sur.
findings.why: I don't know all the US state abbreviations yet, and the map has no place names to help me.
findings.suggestion: The first time each state appears on the Spanish sheet, give its English name and abbreviation: 'Carolina del Sur (South Carolina, SC)', 'Carolina del Norte (North Carolina, NC)', 'Virginia Occidental (West Virginia)'.
findings.evidence: Labels 'NC (1788)', 'NC 12' and 'SC 8' in we-the-people-1787-1791--q4-ratify.png; pop-up title 'North Carolina: 12th state to ratify'

findings.where: q4-nc picture; Population in 1790 and Ratifying the Constitution drawn together; Q4 step 1
findings.what: In this picture there are light-blue pies and dark-blue pies together, and both have orange. Orange means 'Enslaved people' on one and 'Voted against' on the other.
findings.why: If I miss step 1 and leave Population on, I can't tell which pies are votes and which are people.
findings.suggestion: Give the ratification pies a colour pair that isn't used by the population pies, so the two layers can't be mixed up.
findings.evidence: we-the-people-1787-1791--q4-nc.png (light-blue population pies in Maine and Georgia next to the dark-blue ratification pies)

findings.where: The app's side tools; Q1 step 1 ('Abre el marcador The states in 1790'). The same wording is in the elections, Louisiana Purchase and War of 1812 sheets
findings.what: The sheet says 'marcador', but the button in the app says 'Bookmarks'. The sheet gives me the English word for Map layers, Measure and Sketch, but not for this one.
findings.why: I have to try the buttons one by one to find the marcadores.
findings.suggestion: In each sheet, write 'Abre el marcador (Bookmarks) …' the first time a bookmark is used.
findings.evidence: Sheet text; the tools list in the packet names the button Bookmarks. The app's buttons are not shown in the pictures

rights-and-responsibilities-where-we-liv.works: The district pop-up is one short sentence with the name in bold ('Mike Carey (Republican) represents Ohio Congressional District 15'), and the clicked district lights up, so I can answer the first part of Q1 quickly. The Topographic basemap has place names, so I can find my own town.

findings.where: Topographic basemap zoomed into a town (q4-nrhp shows the street-level view); Q2 (Derechos en lugares públicos) steps 1–2 and Q3 step 1
findings.what: The sheet lists tribunal, ayuntamiento, biblioteca, lugar de culto, centro de votación and redacción de un periódico. The map will use the English words, like Courthouse, City Hall, Library, Church or Post Office. 'Library' looks like 'librería' but means biblioteca. At the zoom in the picture I see streets and neighbourhoods but no building names yet.
findings.why: I won't recognise the English names of the places I'm looking for, and I don't know how far to zoom in.
findings.suggestion: On the Spanish sheet, add the English word the map uses: 'un tribunal (Courthouse), el ayuntamiento (City Hall), una biblioteca (Library; no es librería), un lugar de culto (Church, Mosque, Synagogue, Temple), la redacción de un periódico (newspaper office)'. Say that polling places (centros de votación) usually have no label on the basemap, and say how far to zoom, for example until single buildings appear.
findings.evidence: rights-and-responsibilities-where-we-live--q4-nrhp.png shows a city at street level with no public-building names. No picture shows the closer zoom where building names would appear

findings.where: open and q1-district pictures; Congressional districts (119th Congress); Q1 (¿Quién nos representa?) step 4 and '¿Cuántos distritos tiene tu estado?'
findings.what: All the lines are the same blue, so I can't see where my state ends and the next one starts. In the east the lines are so close they look like one blue patch. The pop-up says 'District 15', but not how many districts Ohio has.
findings.why: To count, I have to know my state's shape and click every district. I might think 'District 15' means there are 15 districts.
findings.suggestion: Add a state boundary layer with a thicker or darker line than the district lines, or add the state's total to the pop-up (for example 'one of N districts in Ohio').
findings.evidence: rights-and-responsibilities-where-we-live--open.png; pop-up text 'Mike Carey (Republican) represents Ohio Congressional District 15'

findings.where: q4-nrhp-click pop-up; National Register of Historic Places; 'Cómo leer el mapa' and Q4 (Historia donde vivimos) step 3
findings.what: The sheet says the pop-up gives an address but no name, and tells me to find the name on the basemap or in the 'National Archive Information' link. But the pop-up shows the name in big letters: 'Ohio Statehouse'. Under it are 'SE corner of High and Broad Sts.', 'Status: Listed' and 'National Register Information Tracking System Reference Number', and the link is cut off at the bottom.
findings.why: The sheet and the map say different things, so I wonder if I clicked the wrong thing. If I follow the sheet, I scroll down to a link to English archive papers I can't read.
findings.suggestion: Change the sheet to 'El título de la ventana emergente da el nombre del lugar' and drop the step about the link. In the pop-up, hide the reference-number lines so the name, address and type come first.
findings.evidence: Pop-up text 'Ohio Statehouse / Property ID: 72001011 / SE corner of High and Broad Sts. …'; rights-and-responsibilities-where-we-live--q4-nrhp-click.png

findings.where: q4-nrhp picture and legend; National Register of Historic Places; Q4 step 4
findings.what: The diamonds are small. In the legend 'district' is brown-red and 'site' is dark red, and 'structure' and 'object' are both pale green-yellow. All the diamonds I can see in Columbus look the same dark green.
findings.why: I can't tell those colours apart on such small diamonds. The pop-up already says 'Resource Type: building', which is easier for me.
findings.suggestion: Change step 4 to: 'Lee la línea Resource Type de la ventana emergente: building (edificio), district (distrito), site (sitio), structure (estructura), object (objeto).'
findings.evidence: Legend swatches in rights-and-responsibilities-where-we-live--q4-nrhp.png; pop-up line 'Resource Type: building'

presidential-elections-1796-1800.works: The pie colours match the sheet (orange for Adams, blue for Jefferson), and the pop-up title gives the state and its electors ('Pennsylvania: 15 electors'). The McCulloch pop-up has a bold 'Why here:' heading that matches the sheet exactly, and when I zoom in the two pink squares are far enough apart to measure.

findings.where: q4-marbury picture (zoomed to Washington and Baltimore); Landmark Supreme Court cases, 1803 and 1819; Q4 (La Corte Suprema, cerca de la capital) steps 1–2
findings.what: I click the pink square labelled 'Marbury v. Madison (1803)' and nothing opens.
findings.why: Without the pop-up I can't read 'Why here' for Marbury, so I can't say what happened at that place. I'll think I'm doing something wrong and keep clicking.
findings.suggestion: Check that pop-ups are turned on for the Marbury feature, and that nothing (the DC outline or the label) sits over its click area. Until it is fixed, put Marbury's 'Why here' text on the sheet.
findings.evidence: presidential-elections-1796-1800--q4-marbury.png; pop-up text '(no pop-up opened)'

findings.where: open and q1-pie pictures (the sixteen states view); Landmark Supreme Court cases drawn over Election of 1796 / 1800; Q1 step 3 and Q2 steps 2–3
findings.what: Near Washington the two pink squares and the label 'Marbury v. Madison (1803)' sit on top of a pie (Maryland). I can't see its colours, and if I click there I may get a square instead of the state. At this zoom the McCulloch label doesn't show.
findings.why: Maryland is one of the states that split its votes, so I could miss it in Q1 and Q2. The map has no state names, so I wouldn't know I'd missed it.
findings.suggestion: Have the court-cases layer off when the map opens and turn it on in Q4, or show it only when zoomed in. Another option is to move the squares so they don't cover the Maryland pie.
findings.evidence: presidential-elections-1796-1800--open.png and presidential-elections-1796-1800--q1-pie.png (squares and label over the pie at Maryland)

findings.where: All election views; Q3 (¿Qué estados cambiaron?) step 3 and the question about Nueva Inglaterra
findings.what: The sheet says 'fíjate en Nueva Inglaterra'. The map has no names, and I don't know which states are New England.
findings.why: I can't say whether a New England state changed if I don't know which pies to look at.
findings.suggestion: On the sheet: 'Nueva Inglaterra (New England): los seis estados pequeños del noreste, arriba a la derecha del mapa.' Or add a 'New England' bookmark.
findings.evidence: presidential-elections-1796-1800--open.png (no place names on the map)

findings.where: q2-1800 picture; Election of 1796 off and Election of 1800 on; Q2 (La elección de 1800) steps 1–3
findings.what: After I switch to 1800, the pop-up I opened before is still there, and it still says 'Electors' votes in 1796: John Adams 1, Thomas Jefferson 14…'.
findings.why: I read slowly and go by the numbers, so I could copy the 1796 numbers as the 1800 answer.
findings.suggestion: Add to the sheet: 'Cierra la ventana emergente (X) antes de cambiar de capa.' Or start each pop-up title with the year: '1800 — Pennsylvania: 15 electors'.
findings.evidence: presidential-elections-1796-1800--q2-1800.png (the 1796 pop-up is open while the 1800 layer is on). The picture also caught the pies changing over (New York's pie is a mix of orange and blue), so I couldn't check the 1800 colours outside New England

findings.where: q4-mcculloch pop-up; Landmark Supreme Court cases; Q4 step 2
findings.what: 'Maryland sued James McCulloch, a cashier at the Baltimore branch of the Bank of the United States, to collect a state tax on the bank.' I don't know 'sued', 'cashier' or 'branch'. 'Why here' is the last part, so I have to scroll to it.
findings.why: This is the sentence I need for my answer, and its three key words are nothing like Spanish.
findings.suggestion: Use simpler English: 'Why here: James McCulloch worked at the national bank's office in Baltimore. Maryland wanted the bank to pay a state tax, so it took him to court.' Or put 'Why here' first. The sheet could also gloss the words: sued = demandó, cashier = cajero, branch = sucursal.
findings.evidence: Pop-up text for McCulloch v. Maryland (1819); presidential-elections-1796-1800--q4-mcculloch.png ('Why here' at the bottom of a box that is cut off)

findings.where: q1-pie pop-up; Election of 1796; Q1 step 3
findings.what: The pop-up names four people (Adams 1, Jefferson 14, Pinckney 2, Burr 13), but the pie has only two colours. It also says '1 votes'.
findings.why: I wonder where Pinckney and Burr are in the pie. The sheet explains the two votes, so I can manage.
findings.suggestion: Change '1 votes' to '1 vote', and add a line such as 'Pinckney and Burr are not shown in the pie.'
findings.evidence: Pop-up text: 'In the pie: John Adams (Federalist), 1 votes; Thomas Jefferson (Democratic-Republican), 14 votes.'

louisiana-purchase-1803-1806.works: The yellow Purchase is big and easy to see, and its pop-up gives both numbers the sheet asks for (530,000,000 acres, $15 million). At the Across the Rockies to the Pacific bookmark I can clearly see where the route leaves the yellow and that the Pacific coast isn't yellow.

findings.where: open picture (legend open) and q1-purchase; Territorial acquisitions to 1803; Q1 (Un país más grande) steps 1–3
findings.what: The sheet says the 1783 land is 'verde'. On the map it's a dark grey-blue-green, and with the legend open most of it is under the legend box. When I click the Purchase, the yellow turns bright green.
findings.why: I use the Spanish colour words to find things. The only bright green I see is the Purchase after I click it, so I could compare the wrong areas when I estimate how much bigger the country got.
findings.suggestion: On the sheet, call it 'gris verdoso oscuro' and add 'cierra la leyenda para ver todo el territorio de 1783'. Or give the 1783 territory a colour that is clearly different from the selection highlight.
findings.evidence: louisiana-purchase-1803-1806--open.png (the legend covers most of the 1783 territory); louisiana-purchase-1803-1806--q1-purchase.png (the selected Purchase is bright green)

findings.where: q2-watersheds and q2-missouri-basin pictures; United States Watersheds; Q2 (¿Por qué Nueva Orleans?) steps 2–3
findings.what: All the outlines are the same brown and many of them are big. There are no river names, so I don't know where the Ohio or the Missouri is. For 'sigue los ríos hasta donde terminan', the rivers are thin, faint lines under the yellow, and the map shows no Mississippi or New Orleans.
findings.why: I can only guess which outlines to click, and I get the answer 'Nueva Orleans' from the sheet's title, not from the map.
findings.suggestion: On the sheet: 'Haz clic en el contorno marrón por donde la ruta sube por el río Misuri, y en el contorno al este, donde la ruta baja desde Pittsburgh por el río Ohio. Luego haz clic en el contorno donde terminan, junto al golfo de México, y lee su nombre.' On the map, add a New Orleans point and label the Mississippi, Missouri and Ohio rivers.
findings.evidence: louisiana-purchase-1803-1806--q2-watersheds.png; pop-up 'Missouri Region / HUC ID: 10' in louisiana-purchase-1803-1806--q2-missouri-basin.png

findings.where: q3-biomes (Up the Missouri bookmark, Biomes on) and q3-biome-click; Biomes, United States Watersheds and Territorial acquisitions to 1803; Q3 (Río Misuri arriba) steps 3–4
findings.what: At the Up the Missouri bookmark I see no biome colours. It's the same yellow as the Purchase, the brown watershed lines are still there, and my click on the route opens 'Souris-Red-Rainy Region, HUC ID: 09, States touched by this HUC' (1 of 3). When I zoom out, the biomes show and the first line says 'Temperate Grasslands, Savannas & Shrublands', but that khaki colour is almost the same as the Purchase yellow.
findings.why: I can't tell whether I'm clicking the biome or the Purchase, and the first pop-up isn't a biome, so I have to use the arrows and read more English.
findings.suggestion: Check that the Biomes layer draws at the Up the Missouri bookmark scale, and that all the watershed sublayers turn off with the group. In step 3, also say 'desactiva Territorial acquisitions to 1803', and add 'Si dice 1 de 3, usa las flechas hasta ver el nombre de un bioma.'
findings.evidence: louisiana-purchase-1803-1806--q3-biomes.png (the map is the same yellow as the Purchase; the watershed pop-up shows '1 of 3'); louisiana-purchase-1803-1806--q3-biome-click.png (the grassland khaki next to the Purchase yellow)

findings.where: q1-purchase, q2-missouri-basin and q3-biome-click (zoomed-out views); Lewis and Clark campsites (approximate) and Lewis and Clark National Historic Trail; Q4 (A través de las Montañas Rocosas) steps 3–4
findings.what: The route line ends in the east, but there are more orange dots further east that aren't on the line. The map doesn't show 'Pittsburgh' anywhere.
findings.why: I don't know which dot is Pittsburgh, so I might measure from the wrong place and get the wrong distance.
findings.suggestion: Add a labelled point for Pittsburgh (or label both ends of the route), or hide the eastern campsites that aren't on the line. On the sheet: 'el extremo este de la línea, no los puntos sueltos más al este'.

findings.where: open and q4-rockies pictures; Lewis and Clark National Historic Trail; 'Cómo leer el mapa' and Q3 step 2
findings.what: The sheet says 'una línea morada', but what I see is an orange line of dots. The purple only shows in small gaps.
findings.why: For a moment I think the route is missing, but I can follow the dots.
findings.suggestion: On the sheet: 'una fila de puntos naranjas (los campamentos) sobre una línea morada'. Or make the trail line thicker or the campsite dots smaller.

findings.where: q2-watersheds legend and the watershed pop-ups; United States Watersheds; Q2 step 2
findings.what: The legend says 'Hydrologic Unit Code 2s', and the pop-ups say 'HUC ID: 10' and 'States touched by this HUC'. I don't know what HUC means.
findings.why: I don't need it for the answer, but words I can't read make me unsure whether I'm on the right layer.

war-of-1812-and-monroe-doctrine.works: The battle colours match the sheet (blue for American, red for British, grey for no winner), and the three biggest diamonds are easy to find at the War of 1812 bookmark. Each battle pop-up puts the date, the winner and the casualties in three short lines at the top, and the treaty-line pop-ups say plainly which river or latitude each part follows ('The Sabine River, from the Gulf of Mexico north to latitude 32° N').

findings.where: Legend 'Total Casualties' (open and q1-bookmark pictures) and the battle pop-ups; Battles of the War of 1812; 'Cómo leer el mapa' and Q2 (Las batallas más grandes)
findings.what: 'Casualties' looks like 'casualidades' (coincidences). The sheet says 'bajas', but it never says that 'casualties' is the English word for it on the map. The smallest size in the legend says '< 0'.
findings.why: If I don't know that casualties means bajas, I don't understand why the diamonds are different sizes or what 'Total Casualties: 2,096' means.
findings.suggestion: On the sheet: 'las bajas (en inglés, casualties: muertos, heridos, capturados o desaparecidos)'. Fix the smallest legend class so it doesn't say '< 0'.
findings.evidence: Legend text 'Total Casualties … < 0' in war-of-1812-and-monroe-doctrine--open.png; pop-up 'Total Casualties: 2,096' (New Orleans)

findings.where: q4-latin and q4-circle pictures; Latin American independence and US recognition; Q4 (Nuevas naciones y la doctrina Monroe) steps 3–4
findings.what: The labels say 'Mexico 1821', 'Chile 1818', 'Buenos Ayres 1816', 'Haiti 1804'. I think those are the years the United States recognised them. But the Buenos Ayres pop-up says independence 1816 and recognition 1/27/1823.
findings.why: The question is about recognition before 2 December 1823. If I use the years on the labels I get wrong answers. Haiti 1804 looks early, but it is an orange 'Recognized later' diamond.
findings.suggestion: Show the recognition year in the labels, or mark the year as independence ('Chile, ind. 1818'). Or add to the sheet: 'El año de la etiqueta es el de la independencia, no el del reconocimiento.'
findings.evidence: war-of-1812-and-monroe-doctrine--q4-latin.png (labels show independence years); pop-up text 'Independence: Declared independence from Spain on 9 July 1816. Recognized by the United States: 1/27/1823'

findings.where: q3-boundary picture (The 1819 boundary bookmark, legend open); Land Spain gave up in 1819 and Adams–Onís Treaty line, 1819; Q3 (Florida y una nueva frontera) steps 3–4
findings.what: At this bookmark I can see the pink dashes in the West, but not the green land, only a tiny green spot in the mountains. Florida and the start of the line at the Gulf of Mexico are behind the legend box on the right, and the legend for the green land is cut off at the bottom.
findings.why: The sheet says 'haz clic en la tierra verde' and I can't find it. I'd click the tiny spot, or think the layer didn't turn on.
findings.suggestion: Make The 1819 boundary bookmark wider so it shows Florida and the whole line from the Gulf to the Pacific, with room for the legend. Or add to the sheet: 'Cierra la leyenda y mueve el mapa hacia el sureste para ver Florida en verde.'
findings.evidence: war-of-1812-and-monroe-doctrine--q3-boundary.png. The green land and the Sabine part of the line show only in the zoomed-out pictures war-of-1812-and-monroe-doctrine--q3-florida.png and war-of-1812-and-monroe-doctrine--q3-treatyline.png

findings.where: q3-florida pop-up; Land Spain gave up in 1819 (East Florida); Q3 step 3 and '¿Qué obtuvo Estados Unidos de España?'
findings.what: 'While the Americans didn't pay Spain for the land, they did agree to assume $5 million in damage caused by American citizens when they rebelled against Spain.' It's one long sentence and I don't understand who rebelled.
findings.why: This is the text I'll use for my answer, so if it's confusing or wrong, my answer will be too.
findings.suggestion: I suspect the meaning is off. Check the treaty text (the Avalon Project copy already linked from the treaty-line pop-up) to see whether the US agreed to pay its own citizens' claims against Spain, up to $5 million, rather than damage done by Americans who rebelled. Then rewrite it in short sentences, for example: 'The United States did not pay Spain for Florida. It agreed to pay American citizens' claims against Spain, up to $5 million.'
findings.evidence: Pop-up text 'East Florida (Spanish Cession) 1819'; war-of-1812-and-monroe-doctrine--q3-florida.png

findings.where: All views, historic basemap labels; 'Cómo leer el mapa' ('El mapa no tiene nombres de lugares') and Q4
findings.what: The sheet says the map has no place names, but I see 'United States', 'New Spain of Mexico', 'Louisiana', 'Cuba' and 'Bahamas'. In South America the map writes 'Perú' in the middle, near the Paraguay diamond, far from the 'Peru 1821' diamond on the coast.
findings.why: The names help me, but seeing Peru in two places confuses me, because I know where Peru is.
findings.suggestion: On the sheet: 'El mapa base tiene algunos nombres históricos de esa época.' Check what the historic 'Perú' label refers to and explain it in a line on the sheet, or use a basemap without it.
findings.evidence: war-of-1812-and-monroe-doctrine--open.png; war-of-1812-and-monroe-doctrine--q4-latin.png (the 'Perú' basemap label near the Paraguay diamond, and the 'Peru 1821' label on the coast)

findings.where: q2-neworleans pop-up; Battles of the War of 1812; Q2 steps 1–2
findings.what: The first three lines are easy: 'January 8, 1815 / American Side Victory / Total Casualties: 2,096'. After them comes a long story, and its last paragraph is printed twice.
findings.why: I read slowly. When I see the same paragraph twice I think I missed something and read it all again.
findings.suggestion: Remove the repeated paragraph from the New Orleans record, and check the other battles for the same repeat.
findings.evidence: Pop-up text for New Orleans: the paragraph starting 'On January 8, 1815, Maj. Gen. Andrew Jackson's hastily assembled army…' appears twice

findings.where: q4-circle pop-up; Latin American independence and US recognition; Q4 steps 3–4
findings.what: Independence is written '9 July 1816', but recognition is '1/27/1823, 12:00 AM'. In Spanish we put the day first, and I don't know why there's a time.
findings.why: I have to compare every date with 2 December 1823. With a date like 8/4/1824 I wouldn't know which number is the month.
findings.suggestion: Write the recognition date in words, like the independence date ('27 January 1823'), and remove '12:00 AM'. The ratification dates in the We the People map ('11/21/1789, 12:00 AM') need the same fix.
findings.evidence: Pop-up text 'Recognized by the United States: 1/27/1823, 12:00 AM'
